title: Trying to make a malaria drug, an 18-year-old chemist made a purple dye instead

cover.alt: Black-and-white portrait photograph of William Henry Perkin in later life, with white hair and a full white beard.

body: In 1856 [William Henry Perkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Perkin), then 18, took up a challenge from his professor, August Wilhelm von Hofmann: to make quinine, an expensive natural malaria drug. He oxidised aniline with potassium dichromate and got a black solid that looked like a failure, but when he cleaned the flask with alcohol he noticed **purple in the solution**. He patented the colour, opened a dyeworks at Greenford the next year, and his ‘aniline purple’, later called mauve, became a fashion craze. It was among the first chemical dyes to be mass-produced, and it launched the synthetic dye industry.

slides.prompt: The young chemist was William Henry Perkin, and his dye was first called aniline purple. Where does its later name, mauve, come from?
slides.answer: The French name for the mallow flower
slides.detail: The name mauve caught on in England in 1859. Chemists later called the dye itself mauveine.

steps.label: Get a black solid: no quinine
Spot a purple solution: a new dye

slides.heading: The mauve measles
slides.text: A similar colour was taken up by Queen Victoria in Britain and by Empress Eugénie in France, and the craze spread so fast that Punch magazine joked: “The Mauve Measles are spreading to so serious an extent…”. By 1870, newer synthetic colours had taken over.

slides.label: the year mauveine’s molecular structure was finally identified
slides.text: Almost 140 years after Perkin made it, chemists showed that mauveine is not one compound but a mixture of four related aromatic compounds.

slides.question: What actually reacted in Perkin’s flask to make the purple dye?
options: Alcohol reacting with the black solid
slides.explanation: The aniline he used contained toluidines as impurities, and these reacted with the aniline to form the purple compounds.
